tasks.extracted: By years of snus use at baseline, all-cause aHR rose from 1.08 (0.88–1.32) under 5 years to 1.29 (1.20–1.38) at 15 years or more (p for trend 0.001); cardiovascular and other-cause deaths showed the same pattern (p for trend 0.001 each), cancer did not (0.11). tasks.locator: Table 2; Discussion, 4th to 7th, 8th and 10th paragraphs
tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC7825961 (all sections, Tables 1 to 4, funding and conflict statements; Figure 1 and any supplementary material not read)
tasks.extracted: The current snus group was younger (mean age 29 against 38 years), drank more (37.9% in the highest alcohol tertile against 20.2%) and more often had 10 to 12 years of education (52.6% against 38.7%) than men who never used tobacco; body mass index was similar (24.1 against 24.6). The authors name residual confounding and a single baseline measurement of exposure as weaknesses, and describe their findings as supporting an association, with public-health relevance if it is causal. Their suggested explanations (nicotine effects on blood vessels and heart rhythm, tumour promotion, poorer cancer survival, alcohol-linked injury and violence, risk-taking) were not tested in these data.

tasks.extracted: The authors' summary: snus probably increases the risk of cancer of the oesophagus and pancreas (moderate certainty), may increase the risk of stomach and rectal cancer (low), and the evidence suggests more cancer deaths and more deaths after a cancer diagnosis (low); they are very uncertain about the other cancers, and do not know the effect in women. tasks.extracted: Studies by researchers linked to the tobacco industry or sponsored by it were excluded by design, as were estimates based only on combined snus and cigarette use. Exposure caveats: a single baseline recording of tobacco habits; about 30% of men using snus only may later stop or move to smoking (a Swedish study cited); more than 75% of men using snus only were under 30 at entry and few were followed beyond 70; seven of the included studies used construction-worker data from 1971 to 1975, when non-use could not be told from non-response; 13.2% of never-smoking men using snus, against 6.7% of men who never used tobacco, had a repeat record showing smoking in one study. All authors declare no conflicts of interest; the page has no funding statement.

tasks.extracted: Funding as printed: intramural funding of the German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR), SFP grant 1322-772. Competing interests: none declared. Not commissioned; externally peer reviewed. All six authors are in the BfR Department of Chemical and Product Safety, Berlin. The institute was asked by the Federal Ministry of Food and Agriculture to assess potential risks of new nicotine pouches. The authors note that most earlier pouch studies were done by manufacturers, for example a study with up to 11.9 mg per pouch and no nitrosamines quantified in four pouches, with a quantification limit of 10 ng per gram that they call less sensitive than theirs.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 5th, 8th and 9th paragraphs; Conclusions, 1st paragraph; Background, 1st to 4th paragraphs
tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC9985244 (all sections, Tables 1 to 6, funding and competing-interest statements; reference list and the cited studies not read)
tasks.extracted: Authors' reading: few constituents at low levels in ZYN, suggesting low toxicity; the data are limited to constituent content, and long-term epidemiological data are needed for a full risk assessment. The Background states that long-term studies have convincingly shown snus to carry substantially fewer adverse effects than smoking (citing one review, which is supported by the same company, see the snus claim) and that tobacco-free pouches should, at least in theory, not expose people to nitrosamines. Only two variants of one brand were tested, one batch each, and no toxicity, uptake or health outcome was measured.

tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC13660210 (author manuscript; main text, funding and interest statements and reference list; Figure 1 and the supplementary zip not read)
tasks.extracted: Nicotine uptake: in an independent German crossover study of adults who smoked daily, a 30 mg pouch gave the highest peak and total nicotine over 4 hours, then a cigarette, then 20 mg and 6 mg pouches (time to peak 5 minutes for the cigarette, 20 minutes for the 6 mg pouch); in adults who used smokeless tobacco daily, 8 mg pouches delivered comparable or more nicotine than smokeless tobacco after 30 minutes of use; in industry-funded series, 4 mg and 8 mg pouches gave lower peak and total nicotine than a cigarette and 12 mg and 8 mg mini-size pouches comparable or higher, with time to peak 35 to 40 minutes against 5 to 7 for a cigarette; in adults who used Swedish snus, peak and 60-minute nicotine from 6, 9 and 11.2 mg pouches were higher than from 11.2 mg snus (twice as high for the 11.2 mg pouch), and pouches delivered nicotine slightly faster than snus and nicotine gum. Four of eight new pharmacokinetic trials were industry-funded (British American Tobacco, Japan Tobacco International). The abstract says uptake from pouches of 6 mg or more typically exceeds that from cigarettes, which the 6 mg result in this section does not show.

tasks.extracted: Pouch evidence base (15 studies): five short crossover trials of 30 to 42 adults (blood pressure, heart rate, craving, abuse potential; one 9-hour trial funded by the manufacturer), a 24-week trial of oral health (n printed as 155; sex counts sum to 100), an 8-week pilot (n = 45), a 6-month online cohort (n = 1,863 at start), a national cohort (n = 5,556), three cross-sectional symptom surveys in Saudi Arabia (n = 489, 1,214, 831) and three Swedish oral-health studies (n = 23 to 272). Search to 25 July 2026, English only; funded by the Medical University of Lodz; no competing interests declared; the review does not report who funded most included studies.

tasks.extracted: Pouch heart and blood pressure effects: in a single-use crossover study of 30 people who use snus or pouches, changes measured 30 minutes after use were, by strength, systolic pressure -1% (6 mg), +3% (9 mg) and +1.4% (11.2 mg), diastolic +4.5%, +7.4% and +3.9%, and heart rate -3%, +3.2% and -0.2%; in a survey with no comparison group 28.4% of people who use pouches reported rapid or irregular heartbeat. The text calls the 11.2 mg product snus and gives its heart-rate change as +0.2%; Table 6 labels it a pouch and gives -0.2%.

tasks.locator: Results › Pouches › Oral Health, 1st paragraph; Table 6
tasks.source_read: Publisher full text (Springer HTML): all sections and Tables 1 to 6, funding and competing-interest statements; Figure 1 and Online Resources 1 and 2 not read
tasks.extracted: Pouch oral findings: among 272 young Swedish adults, oral lesions 79% and hyperkeratosis 65% in people who use pouches (n = 126) against 89% and 79% in people who use snus (n = 63); erythema 44% and mucosal ulcers 2% in the pouch group; gingival recession 45% against 52%. After 23 dentists switched from snus to pouches, snus lesion severity fell from 95.7% to 69.6% and gingival irritation from 43.5% to 4.3%. In a randomized trial of adults who smoked (n printed as 155), gingival and bleeding indices were 20% to 30% lower at 12 and 24 weeks after switching to pouches than with continued smoking (the Altria-funded trial named in the scoping review).

tasks.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph; Conclusions, 1st paragraph
tasks.source_read: Publisher full text (Springer HTML): all sections and Tables 1 to 6, funding and competing-interest statements; Figure 1 and Online Resources 1 and 2 not read
tasks.extracted: Authors' stated limitations: many studies of men only; few data on pouches; self-reported use; no meta-analysis because of heterogeneity; most studies from Scandinavia and Swedish snus differs from products elsewhere; observational designs prevent establishing causality; brands, nicotine content and flavours vary; quality not always satisfactory. Conclusion: too little data to clearly determine the health effects of pouches.
